title: Did Anthropic Miss Its Peak IPO Moment?
summary: It’s beginning to look like Anthropic waited too late to go public. Third-quarter revenue numbers disclosed to investors on Wednesday implied that its growth has slowed from the second quarter, which we reported is likely to put a ceiling on its IPO valuation. Anthropic might have been better off going public in June, when its growth was still spectacular. (Of course, a June IPO might have been impractical given that that’s when SpaceX went public.) As things stand now, Anthropic’s slowing growth may remind investors of a longstanding question surrounding the company: How much of a moat does it really have? Yes, its AI models are as good as they get, but increasingly, businesses don’t need really expensive frontier models. As we wrote earlier this week , developers are increasingly opting for other models that are good enough for most tasks. Anthropic’s aggressive pricing has prompted companies such as Microsoft to cut its spending on the former’s models, we reported 10 days ago . (This trend seems to be spreading ).

title: Singapore’s DayOne Pushes Ahead With Data Center IPO Tied to TikTok
summary: DayOne Data Centers, a Singapore-based data center operator gearing up for a multibillion-dollar initial public offering in New York, is little known to most U.S. investors. But its business is built on a much better known company: ByteDance . The TikTok parent company accounts for nearly 70% of DayOne’s revenue, according to two people with knowledge of DayOne’s operations. DayOne, which started as a Chinese data center company’s overseas business unit four years ago, has benefitted greatly from ByteDance’s rapid global expansion through TikTok. But that has also left it extraordinarily dependent on a single customer, which the company has acknowledged creates a significant risk for its business.

title: Apple’s Antitrust Settlement Talks Spur Worries Among Developers

Several developers, including PayPal and Epic Games, have discussed their concerns with the Justice Department about a possible settlement of the Apple case, the people said. In communication with developers, Justice Department officials have signaled their preference to settle the lawsuit rather than fight it, the people said.

title: The Party Is Still Going Strong for Private Tech
summary: The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds , a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator. Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown. This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors. “You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference.
